title: How Do Rockets Fly? Science for Kids with Gizmo
description:
How do rockets fly? Find out with Gizmo the robot: a rocket engine turns its fuel into hot gas and pushes it out the back, and the gas pushes the rocket the other way. A rocket carries its own oxygen, so it works in space, and big rockets drop empty stages to get lighter.
A science explainer for kids ages 4-8, with questions to answer, things to copy, quick checks and a quiz at the end.

Where the facts come from (read Nov 19, 2026): NASA, What Is a Rocket? (Grades K-4 and Grades 5-8); NASA Glenn Research Center, Practical Rocketry.
facts: NASA, 'What Is a Rocket? (Grades K-4)', nasa.gov/learning-resources/for-kids-and-students/what-is-a-rocket-grades-k-4 (read Nov 19 2026): 'Most rocket engines turn the fuel into hot gas.' 'The engine pushes the gas out its back.' 'The gas makes the rocket move forward.' 'for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.' 'The rocket pushes the exhaust backward.' 'The exhaust makes the rocket move forward.' 'A rocket engine doesn't need air.' 'It carries with it everything it needs.' 'A rocket engine works in space, where there is no air.'

NASA, 'What Is a Rocket? (Grades 5-8)', nasa.gov/learning-resources/for-kids-and-students/what-is-a-rocket-grades-5-8 (read Nov 19 2026): 'A jet engine requires oxygen from the air to work.' 'A rocket engine carries everything it needs.'

NASA Glenn Research Center, 'Practical Rocketry', grc.nasa.gov/www/K-12/rocket/TRCRocket/practical_rocketry.html (read Nov 19 2026): 'for burning to take place, an oxidizer (oxygen) must be present.' 'they must carry oxygen with them into space, where there is no air.' 'When the large rocket was exhausted, the rocket casing was dropped behind and the remaining rocket fired.' 'Much higher altitudes were achieved by this method.' 'Today this technique of building a rocket is called staging.' 'Thanks to staging, it has become possible not only to reach outer space but the Moon and other planets too.' 'the heavier the rocket, the more the thrust needed to get it off the ground.'
improves: first Gizmo explainer: Gizmo hosts in his own lab and outdoor places (gizmoworld set), the example is a science model on the board (rocket with gas puffs, fuel and oxygen tanks, three-stage rocket that drops a stage)
the quiz is three answer-sign rounds with thinking dots and confetti (teach board), so no check mark has to stand beside a face (open Zoo defect: quiz close-ups cut the neighbour)
every example cued on the word that names it; no close-up while an example is up
no real people named (the push-back rule is 'a rule scientists use', not a name), no fire shown (soft gas puffs), nothing to copy but hand and breathing moves

segments.name: hello
lines: Hello, friends! I am Gizmo the robot.
Today we are finding out how rockets fly!
My little helper bot is here too. Hello, little bot!
We have three big questions. Count them with me. One, two, three!
Ready? Let's find out!

segments.name: push

lines.t: What pushes a rocket up, up into the sky?
Is it hot gas? Or is it the wind?

lines: It is hot gas!
Here is how it works. A rocket engine turns its fuel into hot gas.
The engine pushes the gas out of its back. Whoosh! And the gas pushes the rocket the other way.

lines.t: So which way does the rocket go? Hmm.

lines: The gas goes down, so the rocket goes up!
Whoosh, the gas goes down. Zoom, the rocket goes up!
Up, up, up it goes!
close:host
Scientists have a rule about pushes.
For every push, there is a push back, just as big, the other way!
A big push down makes a big push up!
The rocket pushes the gas backward. The gas pushes the rocket forward.
A push, and a push back. That is how a rocket moves!
Say it with me. The gas goes down, the rocket goes up!
close:host
Can you press your hands together? Push! Can you feel them push back?
Push, and push back. Now let your hands rest.

lines.t: Quick check! The gas goes down. Which way does the rocket go? Up? Or down?

lines: Up! Great thinking!

short.title: What Pushes a Rocket Up? Science for Kids
short.fact: A rocket engine turns its fuel into hot gas and pushes it out the back; the gas pushes the rocket the other way (NASA, What Is a Rocket?).

segments.name: space

lines.t: Can a rocket work in space, where there is no air?
Is it yes? Or is it no?

lines: Yes, it can!
Even way up in space!
Here is the fun fact. A rocket engine does not need air.
It carries everything it needs, right inside the rocket!

lines.t: What does a rocket carry? Hmm.

lines: Its fuel, and its very own oxygen! The fuel needs oxygen to work.
Fuel and oxygen, packed in two big tanks.
Ready for the trip to space!
close:host
An airplane's jet engine is different.
A jet engine takes the oxygen it needs from the air around it.
But up in space, there is no air at all.
In space, there is nothing for an engine to push against, either.
So a rocket brings its own oxygen along. Smart rocket!
Say it with me. A rocket carries its own oxygen!
close:host
Can you take a big breath of air, like a jet engine? Breathe in!
And breathe out, nice and slow. Ahh.

lines.t: Quick check! Does a rocket need air from outside to work? Yes? Or no?

lines: No! It brings its own oxygen. You remembered!

short.title: Can a Rocket Work in Space? Science for Kids
short.fact: A rocket engine does not need air: it carries everything it needs, its fuel and its own oxygen (NASA, What Is a Rocket?; NASA Glenn, Practical Rocketry).

segments.name: stages

lines.t: Why do some big rockets drop parts as they fly?
To get lighter? Or to get heavier?

lines: To get lighter!
Here is the fun fact. Big rockets are built in parts, called stages, stacked one on top of another.
Let's count the stages. One, two, three!
Three stages, stacked up tall!

lines.t: What happens when the bottom stage uses up its fuel? Hmm.

lines: It drops away, and the next stage takes over!
Bye-bye, stage one! Now the rocket is lighter.
close:host
A heavier rocket needs a bigger push to fly.
So dropping the empty part helps the rocket go much higher.
Lighter means it can climb higher, and higher!
This idea is called staging. It helps rockets reach space, and even the Moon!
Up, up, and away. All the way to space!
Say it with me. Rockets drop stages to get lighter!
close:host
Can you stack your fists, one on top of the other, like rocket stages?
Now take the bottom one away. Bye-bye, stage one!

lines.t: Quick check! After a stage drops away, is the rocket lighter? Or heavier?

lines: Lighter! Super thinking!

short.title: Why Do Big Rockets Drop Parts? Science for Kids
short.fact: Big rockets are built in stages; an empty stage is dropped behind and the next one fires, and this staging helps rockets reach space (NASA Glenn, Practical Rocketry).

segments.name: quiz
lines: Wow! We found out so much today. Now it is quiz time!
Get ready. Think hard!

lines.t: Question one. What does a rocket engine push out of its back? Hot gas? Or water?

lines: Hot gas! Yes!

lines.t: Question two. Does a rocket carry its own oxygen? Yes? Or no?

lines: Yes! That's right!

lines.t: Question three. When a stage drops away, is the rocket lighter? Or heavier?

lines: Lighter! You remembered!

segments.name: goodbye
lines: You found out so much today.
The gas goes down, and the rocket goes up. It carries its own oxygen. And it drops stages to get lighter!
What would you like to find out next?
Thank you for exploring with me. Bye-bye, friends! See you next time!
